Replay

Paired game ports and comparison protocol

21 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓

Both framework implementations and both versions of every ported game must remain available. A port is a new project with a separate launch command, save namespace, cache/build output, and network defaults. It never overwrites the original project's gameplay or turns its original runner into a compatibility shim.

The three-profile Cavecrawl cohort adds a quiet two-player comparison of Kit, Replay server motion and Replay owner motion. Nine pairs pass a common movement/interaction contract with separate visible/confirmed timing. Owner motion approaches Kit's responsiveness here while retaining substantially higher application traffic and callback cost. The measured scope, isolated Kit reference-release overlay and superseded first contract are explicit; source counts are not a human usability score.

The current public-history cohort passes the full 24-window native comparison and 64 report checks. It records lower Replay host traffic with continued client CPU cost, and distinguishes the isolated Kit control, content/prediction differences and separate browser TURN conditions. It is the latest loaded Scrapyard native cost baseline, not a declaration of full library readiness.

The observation encoding A/B then measures a targeted optimization on one owner-profile binary: raw and compact modes keep the same accepted workload, cadence and recovery settings. Median client application traffic drops 41.7%; no downstream or total-CPU improvement is claimed.

The recent-fact encoding A/B then shares repeated bundle headers on the downstream path. Six same-binary cases retain the workload, cadence, full occurrences and backups; median host application traffic drops 30.6%, from 9.869 to 6.849 KiB/s. Client traffic is essentially unchanged, and callback measurements do not establish a CPU improvement. The quiet-world cost gap, broader comparisons and adoption decision remain open.

See roadmap for dependencies and architecture for the frame contract.

The P2P live rejoin gate adds recovery evidence for the separate Duel: one participant restores while survivors retain their live runners. This validates a bounded recovery capability; it is not a paired Kit performance measurement or a general stale-save recovery guarantee. The browser extension of that gate uses the real Save & pause button and file import in separate Chrome processes, with only the returning participant killed and restarted. The authenticated P2P extension verifies fixed-roster credentials before binding, including negative admission cases and a three-member signaling mesh. This is capability evidence, not a framework performance comparison. The creator-recovery gate now retains the joining player while creator ID 1 returns under a new connection generation, with retired transport buffers fenced.

The spectator source-failover gate adds continuity-checked replacement of a viewing source while players continue. It preserves spectator state/events and rejects missing or conflicting anchors. This is native and cross-target capability evidence, not a paired Kit performance result or public spectator-authentication claim.

The native creator-return gate adds transport replacement when the saved listening participant returns. It preserves the survivor's runner/frontiers and verifies continued reference gameplay. This is fixed-roster recovery evidence, not a new authority election or a paired framework performance measurement.

The native-generation gate adds connection metadata and queued-packet fencing to the shared Godot adapter, with real ENet, Steam API-contract and native rejoin checks. This is transport correctness evidence, not a new paired performance or live Steam-account result.

The action-intent authoring slice replaces Scrapyard's manual ticket bookkeeping with a reusable helper that also handles recovery dispositions and epoch-scoped sequence reuse. Mechanical source counts and functional gates are recorded separately from human usability and paired runtime performance conclusions.

The endurance workload adds injury/healing, surge, dash and reload. Twelve delay-condition windows pass; the raw-loss condition remains a failed gate for missing short input edges. Its raw observations are retained separately from the accepted performance comparison.

The input-frontier audit fixes the observed Replay dash loss. The latest raw-loss Replay scope passes; the paired condition is rejected for a Kit cast refusal. Scoped acceptance never substitutes for a complete paired result.

The cast-submission correction separates Kit local prediction from actual command submission. It corrects the prior refusal diagnosis; a fresh raw-loss cohort still fails gameplay/observation gates and is not presented as an accepted paired performance result.

The latest endurance cohort passes both conditions: 24 process windows and 56 report cases. It follows the explicit resync-queue implementation and separate branch tests. Prior failures and temporal costs remain recorded; this is one supported workload, not a general adoption result.

The separate jam-clearing workload passes twelve delay-condition windows and 60 report checks, including seeded dud/shot and clear-pull accounting. Its full matrix is rejected for stale Kit cooldown observations and a lost Replay dash under raw loss. The accepted subset and failed cohort remain distinct from the earlier jam-disabled endurance result.

The dash-action port confirms all 120 local Replay dash requests in a new full cohort, with a separate sequence audit proving successful late arrivals. The paired workload remains rejected because three Replay games fall below its kill-count requirement. Delivery acceptance does not replace matched workload or responsiveness evidence.

The subsequent aim-origin correction fixes the stress helper's use of an older local-body position. Its fresh delay condition passes twelve windows and 61 report cases. A ballistic ledger accounts for the earlier low kill output; the raw-loss condition still fails observation freshness. No collision/damage rule or acceptance threshold was relaxed.

The snapshot-ACK result demonstrates ACK-induced action blocking and removes that dependency. Replay passes its fresh delay/raw-loss scope, while paired raw-loss acceptance still fails for a Kit client observation. The paired delay result and controlled ENet regression remain distinct from full-matrix acceptance and general responsiveness claims.

Baseline inventory#

Source revisions inspected when this experiment was created:

  • odin_godot: 13e7d946223745711fbaafe161c46b204fd38b80.
  • Scrapyard sibling repository: 6bdef4f437d9a4e2c98f1d49472f840879301ccf; its working tree was clean at inspection.

These identify source baselines, not benchmark results. Record the actual old and new revisions, dirty diff, dependency versions, and content hashes for every subsequent comparison. Existing projects remain in place; pin a temporary baseline checkout when source changes would otherwise invalidate paired runs.

Existing project New project path What it tests Port status
hello_net, hello_sim replay_hello Common offline/network gameplay, movement, spawn/join, presentation Offline views and initial real-process networking tested
Cavecrawl Replay Cavecrawl Doors, contested loot, inventory, AI, progression, recovery Full normal/faulted gameplay campaign and recovery slices tested; complete authored/UI parity pending
Slopball, Slopball3D examples/replay_slopball/, examples/replay_slopball3d/ Owner authority, Godot physics, control handoff 2D/3D native session/social/rejoin UI and separate solver/network/migration gates pass; fuller parity pending
Quickdraw examples/replay_quickdraw/ Prediction, hitscan rewind, spawning, competitive rules Initial duel/lob/boots, archive and live combat migration gates; full parity/comparison pending
Speedball Replay Speedball Full-world contested ball, spikes, goals and correction smoothing Native contested-ball, UI, migration, restart/saves and native/browser party flows pass; public deployment/visual review pending
Claimball Replay Claimball Local/shared prediction group and claim-weighted presentation Group/claim contests, native/browser menus and saves, Party migration/restore tested; intermittent faults and broader parity/comparison remain open
Workspace sibling ../scrapyard/ Replay Scrapyard Full-game complexity, content, sustained churn, migration Arena/staging, stock combat, abilities, run loop, profiles and initial run/Room recovery; full-game and paired comparison pending

examples/replay_loot/ is the first new runnable headless experiment. It borrows the contested-loot scenario from Cavecrawl but is not a Cavecrawl port and does not yet exercise a network. No full-game parity result is claimed.

Preservation and content rules#

  1. Keep the old project and its run/test commands. A new implementation uses its new path and explicitly imports godot:replay.
  2. Share assets only through a deliberate, versioned content boundary. A shared mutable resource/configuration must not let one game silently alter the other. Copy small assets or use a pinned asset package for independently runnable exports.
  3. Preserve attribution/licenses and record asset/content hashes. No need to copy generated DLLs, addons, node_modules, caches, or exported bundles.
  4. Keep per-game save/profile names distinct. Comparison harnesses run scratch project copies with isolated user data and ports. They must not clear a developer's existing profiles to obtain repeatable tests.
  5. A shared test driver may send the same gameplay intent to each game through thin adapters. It must not replace gameplay logic with a comparison-only path.
  6. If the new framework changes gameplay rules, network trust, physics, tick rate, or content, mark the scenario unmatched until the difference is accounted for.

The original Scrapyard run.sh currently clears persistent profile files during setup. Do not execute it unmodified against personal data as part of a benchmark; establish isolated scratch runs first. Its source was inspected here, not run.

Scrapyard acceptance inventory#

The inspected original harness contains these acts. Use their assertions as behavioral specifications, and add corresponding Replay fixtures as each slice lands.

Original acts New acceptance focus
duo, solo, server Seed/content agreement, seat control, mode parity
guns, combo, lance Cadence/reload, weapon variants, statuses, lag compensation
run, boss, gauntlet Wave progression, transitions, boss state, long-run stability
vault, doppelganger Persistence, stable identity, duplicate-seat behavior
succession Abrupt host loss, restored director state, reseating, continued play
stress Fire volume, entity churn, CPU, memory, bandwidth
spray, mod Asset transfer, compatibility/version decisions, late join
chain, delivery, zone Multi-entity effects and delayed consequences
storm, surge, mend Area effects, sustained combat, healing and attribution

The full-game port should also test migration during these behaviors, even where the original migration act only covers a simpler case. Record a parity matrix with unstarted, implemented, headless-tested, and playtested independently.

Scenario matrix#

Apply this matrix to each port where meaningful. Fault schedules should be seeded and recorded, not just random per-run percentages.

Scenario Conditions Assertions/measurements
Offline reference Same inputs/content/tick rate Correct game rules, reproducibility, authored-code comparison
Local network Host/client/observer, no injected faults Agreement, correct authority and seat identity
Latency 0, 60, 120, 240 ms RTT Input-to-visible delay, correction magnitude, effects timing
Jitter and loss Seeded jitter, 1%/5% loss, short loss bursts Convergence, held-input behavior, missing/duplicate effects
Disorder Duplicated/reordered packets Deduplication and monotonic protocol state
Long blackout Beyond input/history capacity Explicit stall/resync behavior and time to playable recovery
Join/rejoin Mid-action, mid-wave, after disconnect State completeness, identity, no historic cosmetic replay
Contested action Both players take/hit/claim together Conservation, winner rule, reversible feedback
Host migration Planned handoff, crash, successor loss Interruption, lost ticks, duplicated actions, resumed gameplay
Content mismatch Different schema/content/config version Clear rejection before live state mutation
Sustained workload Same entity population/action trace p50/p95/p99 CPU, memory, bytes, replay depth

RTT is round-trip time. The existing shims may specify per-direction latency; record the actual injected parameters and measured RTT so a nominal "120 ms" test cannot accidentally compare 120 ms RTT with 240 ms RTT.

Measures#

Authoring and maintenance#

  • Handwritten gameplay and handwritten framework wiring separately; exclude generated code and report content/UI separately.
  • Number of places changed to implement the same feature: add a weapon, transfer an item, spawn an effectful entity, add a replay-dependent status, persist a director field, and migrate during an ability.
  • Explicit authority/time branches and callbacks an author must understand. Count them as evidence, not a target to game by hiding decisions in wrappers.
  • Time to identify and fix a seeded issue; number and quality of diagnostics.
  • Qualitative port notes: awkward ownership, excessive declarations, missing game primitives, and where the new model is less convenient.

Runtime and player experience#

  • Simulation, snapshot, presentation, and replay CPU separated; p50/p95/p99 and worst replay burst, with warm-up excluded.
  • Resident/peak bytes, bytes per stored frame, history length, and allocations per normal tick and correction.
  • Application and transport bytes per peer by message class, join/checkpoint size, send frequency, and ingress/outbound queue pressure.
  • Input-to-visible response, correction distance/angle, correction frequency, speculative effect duration, cancellation frequency, missing/duplicate effects.
  • Migration interruption and rollback distance, checkpoint age, reconnect/resync time, and preservation of persistent/session outcomes.
  • Human paired playtests, with network conditions and game-rule differences disclosed. A numerically converged game can still feel worse.

Result format and reproducibility#

Store runs under ignored tests/.logs/replay-comparison/; promote selected summaries and machine-readable data to a documented results directory after review. The harness should capture:

Text
scenario and seed
old/new repository revision and dirty diff
Odin, Godot, compiler flags, platform, CPU, render settings
content and gameplay configuration hashes
runner/topology/trust profile, players/entities, tick and send rates
input trace and complete network fault schedule
history, prediction, interpolation, and checkpoint settings
warm-up, repetitions, raw samples, percentile method
scenario invariants and explicit parity gaps

Use repeated paired runs on the same machine and alternate run order. Report raw data and variability; avoid drawing conclusions from a single best run. Measure optimized builds for performance and keep debug/diagnostic overhead separately.

For host migration, do not describe survival from a recent checkpoint as zero lost progress. For deterministic P2P, actual execution and matching logical hashes on each target are required; successful cross-compilation is not that evidence.

Decision record#

For each completed port, publish: which gameplay became simpler, what new constraints appeared, the latency/performance tradeoffs, unresolved failures, and whether the next port is justified. Keep the raw scenarios usable even if the experiment's final outcome is to retain both frameworks for different games.

Active range comparison#

The paired harness now includes a stationary firing/reload scenario alongside the idle arena. Each game uses the same bolter settings and accepts exactly nine rounds per player. Both real input and weapon paths run; a sampled trace records different firing/reload times and projectile occupancy instead of presuming them equal. Three alternating pairs and source/build hashes are required for a comparison result. This adds active weapon work; AI/damage/movement stress, further ports and human playtests remain separate requirements of M9.

Active combat encounter comparison#

The combat harness now adds four explicit stock-enemy spawn requests, live AI approach/bites, target-seeking fire, damage/death and scrap collection. Its shared driver requires matching final kill, damage, pickup and shot totals while recording different player health, attribution, NPC positions/occupancy and timing. Spawning/targeting run inside each measured game callback. An additional read-only census is measured separately.

This advances full-combat evidence beyond the firing range. It does not complete the remaining sustained stress, movement/status/migration comparisons, other ports, authoring-change measurements or paired human playtests. Exact gameplay parity is not inferred from matching aggregate totals.

Measured snapshot scan optimization#

The scan result pairs independent byte-format oracles and executed native/WASM equivalence with six input-density microbenchmarks, three real combat pairs and a separate phase diagnostic. Canonical hashes and delta bytes remain identical. Long zero/equal regions improve, with a retained fragmented-input regression. Host callback cost falls in the new cohort; client median changes little and the overall Kit/Replay cost gap remains. Wider stress/latency and authoring comparisons remain required for an adoption decision.

Compatibility authoring example#

The recorded spread-hop change adds one explicit Flash discriminator without widening world bytes. Preserving older saves still required an old-world descriptor and field mapping (112 lines), CLI routing and historical/fresh-resume validation. This is concrete compatibility work beyond gameplay code; it is not a timed comparison against Kit. Include it in the remaining M9 authoring/API evaluation before claiming singleplayer-like change effort or deciding to adopt the framework.

Executable authoring change: paid revive#

The paid-revive experiment installs the same cross-player wallet/health rule into isolated Kit and Replay copies, preserves the actual feature patches and runs a shared three-player contract. The first full matrix covers funded, funding-while-held and contended revives locally and with receive delay. It separates source-change evidence from sampled replication behavior and explicitly excludes human productivity claims. The harness rebuilds both playable variants; other feature changes and authoring/debugging measurements remain required.

Executable authoring change: existing-family weapon#

The weapon experiment adds one identical resource in both games, with no handwritten gameplay/network changes. Replay's separate generated stock table is recorded as derived work. Independently built clients without the resource receive the host's definition and use it for selection, presentation, damage and reloads. This complements the paid-revive case; it does not measure human authoring time or a new weapon family's cost.

Sustained offensive population comparison#

The swarm harness keeps forty stock scrapbots active for twenty seconds with ordinary combat/pickups and replenishment. Shared zero-bite and large-magazine fixtures prevent player wipes/reload pauses. Three alternating pairs and twenty report checks pass with 38–40 living enemies, measured turnover, authority conservation and converged final peer state.

The result reports callback cost, application output, instrumented RSS and receive freshness. Large snapshots awaiting acknowledgment leave authority frames behind received facts; a separate diagnostic hit a presentation error during fill. Both remain readiness findings. Versioned contracts and rejected cohorts are retained. This advances sustained offensive evidence; movement, statuses/abilities, player damage, faults and full-game/human comparisons remain distinct requirements.

Snapshot delivery tradeoff#

Snapshot parts repeat the same swarm contract after adding negotiated bounded unreliable delivery for large state. Median/p95 extra lag behind received facts falls from 9/17 ticks to 4–5/6, while Replay host output rises from about 43 KB/s to 263 KB/s and client correction work increases. Kit remains lower in callback and traffic cost. The retained artifacts include the controlled delivery comparison, current cohort, old/new protocol interoperability and actual browser part counters. This is measured progress with visible costs; payload reduction, sustained real faults and the full adoption gate remain requirements.

Canonical payload attribution and compression#

The payload/codec result attributes exact sparse delta bytes to state groups, then compares lossless encodings while retaining all history/query data. The selected age-sixteen payload falls from about 9,774 to 6,969 bytes. Native/WASM and reference checks preserve decoded bytes; the repeated swarm reaches 3/4-tick median/p95 extra lag behind received facts. Host output stays near its configured budget and client correction work increases. Source/build identity, initial/final cohorts, rejected prototypes and mixed-peer browser evidence are retained; this is not a full adoption or human-responsiveness verdict.

Raw-UDP fault envelope#

The native ENet fault matrix adds packet-level loss/jitter/duplication and a bounded rate/queue model to the sustained Replay offensive swarm. Both conditions pass twice with final state convergence, packet accounting and explicitly allowed recovery intervals. It is Replay acceptance, not a paired Kit benchmark. The evidence includes the corrected token-bucket proxy, rejected initial runs, sender/timing/fact-delivery changes and browser/migration follow-up. Full mixed gameplay, wider platforms/routes and adoption remain separate requirements.

Speedball session/social port#

The separate Speedball UI result adds direct session menus, validated names, host-only start, chat/input capture, held scores/telemetry and leave/rejoin handling. Existing solo/contested-ball rules and response gates still pass. Native captures provide initial layout evidence; the port ledger retains trust/timeline differences and unimplemented paths. This is port acceptance, not a paired authoring-time or performance result.

Speedball native Room integration#

The Speedball migration result exercises a nonzero score and moving ball through planned handoff and abrupt host loss. The successor restores the exact prepared frame; surviving peers agree on a later canonical world after two fresh spikes and new-epoch chat. Rendered native captures cover the handoff/recovery UI. Existing direct-session and contested-ball gates remain separate checks.

This is a functional Replay port result, not a matched Kit/Replay timing study. Reported interruption is the Room driver's local recovery interval; it excludes some time before failure detection and must not be described as total outage. The fixed local roster/credentials do not establish public enrollment or discovery.

Speedball match and local identity lifecycle#

The round/profile result adds a validated Play again command and native reconnect/name profiles. Three peers finish two matches in one session, reject a guest restart, retain their roster and resume chat. A killed client is replaced by a fresh process using its persisted identity, which must reclaim seat 2 and the chosen name. Corrupt-profile cases preserve the files; deterministic token overrides bypass profile storage.

Original Speedball inherits persistent reconnect identity from Kit boot. Its game scripts do not supply restart or match save/load menus. Play again and persisted display names are added Replay behavior; this result is not evidence of a matched legacy authoring/runtime comparison. The subsequent save/discovery result below supplies the native direct-session save/resume flow.

Speedball save/resume and direct epoch query#

The save/discovery result restores a scored, moving pitch in fresh solo and host processes, then admits a fresh client through the normal Join flow. The new opt-in query learns a direct host's epoch before the existing strict handshake; no epoch number is supplied by the harness. Wrong-profile and damaged/missing archives fail before creating a session. Continued spikes, match completion, restart and chat pass after restore.

This fills a Replay lifecycle flow, not an original Speedball save-menu parity claim or a Kit/Replay timing comparison. Room retains coordinator-controlled recovery; direct file resume does not elect or fence competing hosts. Browser saves and public-room integration remain separate work.

Speedball native parties and observers#

The native party result adds the shared Party helper to Speedball's scene. Verified WSS enrollment and private credential storage precede Room admission; personal identity/name storage stays separate. Planned handoff and owner loss restore a moving scored checkpoint, then a fresh former-host process rejoins the same seat with a stable invite and newer incarnation. The observer remains seat 0, receives no checkpoint and can leave/rejoin in that mode. New spikes/chat and a common later world are required among the final trio.

The Room driver had forced joining members to the player role. It now preserves an explicit Observer request. This result covers that native lifecycle; it does not establish observer invitation permission isolation, browser/Steam behavior, Internet reachability or a comparative authoring/performance advantage over Kit.

Speedball browser party lifecycle#

The Chrome/WebRTC result ports the same scene/model/Party flow to a Web export. Personal identity/name and room credentials persist separately. Planned handoff and host-browser closure restore an exact moving/scored checkpoint; a true observer leaves/rejoins, and the former host returns in a fresh browser process with the same identity/name/invite/seat. New spikes/chat precede a common retained canonical world on all three clients.

This is local browser functional evidence, not a native/browser determinism claim or Kit/Replay performance comparison. The gate does not cover public TLS/TURN, raw network faults, OS-kill durability or other browser engines. Those remain separate requirements along with browser saves and broader playtest coverage.

Speedball browser solo saves#

The browser save result adds named, identity-scoped IndexedDB slots through the existing Browser_Checkpoint adapter. A completed save survives a killed Chrome process, restores exactly, continues gameplay and restarts into round 2. Stale tabs cannot replace a newer revision; damaged archive/identity records remain intact, and a different slot can be used for new play. Native saves and browser parties remain regression gates.

This measures local process-crash recovery and explicit storage failure behavior, not a Kit/Replay timing advantage, power-loss guarantee or general browser-storage availability. Room save publication, other browsers and broader deployment/ playtest/comparison requirements remain.

Moving/status swarm comparison#

The mixed cohort measures three alternating Kit/Replay pairs using the existing replenished forty-enemy fixture, cardinal player movement and stock frostwave/battlecry casts. All twelve processes pass population/freshness, status/cooldown exposure, movement, conservation and settled-peer convergence checks; thirty report acceptance/rejection cases pass.

Median p95 callbacks are 791/656 µs for Kit host/client and 1,901/3,229 µs for Replay. Median application output is about 30,856/2,092 B/s and 252,362/17,583 B/s, respectively. Replay clients remain at p95 five extra fact-lag ticks with no measurement resync. Movement paths and kills differ; this is an identical intent/ fixture envelope with measured outcomes, not identical execution or a framework-only ratio. Kit remains cheaper in these inclusive callback/traffic measurements. The result advances the mixed-workload gate without settling the full M9 adoption case.

Owner-unwind qualification of the mixed cohort#

The causal control identifies a reproduced Kit defect behind the mixed cohort's second-player movement loss. Pending-command delta unwind restores an older owner-streamed position. An engine-free case fails at x=100 instead of 140; an isolated owner-preserving control passes it and all 58 existing Kit networking tests. Three live original/control pairs show 401–442 backward packet-processing moves per original client and zero under the control. The movement step itself never reverses the active input.

Original game/framework sources remain preserved. Earlier costs are still the observations of those binaries, but now carry this explicit baseline qualification. The instrumented control is not a replacement timing cohort. Further comparison with a corrected baseline, plus remaining gameplay/transient differences, is needed before attributing costs or choosing adoption.

Mixed comparison with the isolated owner-unwind repair#

The corrected-baseline cohort uses the copied Kit repair from the movement audit and the normal mixed benchmark adapters, with no extra packet-bracketing instrumentation. Replay uses the original collection root. Twelve process windows and thirty-five report validation cases pass; the declared collection/source control is checked explicitly.

No backward owner motion occurs in the corrected Kit client traces. Median p95 callbacks are 899/804 µs for Kit host/client and 2,024/3,467 µs for Replay; application output is about 29,110/2,092 B/s and 252,349/17,645 B/s. Player travel is much closer than in the defective baseline, while shots, kills and timeline observations still differ. The cost gap persists in this supported envelope; it remains an inclusive product-workload result, not a framework-only ratio or a final adoption decision. Original Kit and game sources stay untouched.

Staged LZ4 encoding follow-up#

The staging result replaces two encoder search passes with one pass into bounded scratch and a final copy. It retains exact wire bytes and atomic output failure, with 65,808 additional workspace bytes. The corrected mixed cohort passes again: Replay host median p95 is 1,845 µs versus 2,024 in the preceding cohort. Host p50 does not improve, and separate instrumented whole-frame means vary upward even while snapshot-delta work falls from 401.1 to 301.9 µs. The result is a targeted encoder improvement, not a uniform game speedup.

Exact correction reuse experiment#

The reuse result verifies an explicit fast path for byte-identical predecessor states and rewritten inputs. A matching 64 KiB synthetic state improves substantially, but the mixed cohort reuses only 111–133 correction records per client alongside roughly 9,925 simulated ticks. Client p95 is 3,266 µs versus 3,273 in the preceding cohort, so no broad workload speedup is established. It stays opt-in; atomic correction, event handling and ordinary audit/full-replay behavior remain separately checked.
